Enhancing aviation safety: A Semantic-Aware Siamese Network for fine-grained readback error detection in air traffic control
A belief-gated defense architecture for 5G cloud-native incomplete information games
The price of decentralization in managing engineering systems through multi-agent reinforcement learning
abstract: Inspection and maintenance (I&M) planning involves sequential decision making under uncertainties and incomplete information, and can be modeled as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). While single-agent deep reinforcement learning provides approximate solutions to POMDPs, it does not scale well in multi-component systems. Scalability can be achieved through multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL), which decentralizes decision-making across multiple agents, locally controlling individual components. However, this decentralization can induce cooperation pathologies that degrade the optimality of the learned policies. To examine these effects in I&M planning, we introduce a set of deteriorating systems in which redundancy is varied systematically. These benchmark environments are designed such that computation of centralized (near-)optimal policies remains tractable, enabling direct comparison of solution methods. We implement and benchmark a broad set of MADRL algorithms spanning fully centralized and decentralized training paradigms, from value-factorization to actor-critic methods. Our results show a clear effect of redundancy on coordination: MADRL algorithms achieve near-optimal performance in series-like settings, whereas increasing redundancy amplifies coordination challenges and can lead to optimality losses. Nonetheless, decentralized agents learn structured policies that consistently outperform optimized heuristic baselines, highlighting both the promise and current limitations of decentralized learning for scalable maintenance planning.
keywords: Decentralized partially observable Markov decision processes

title: Positioning Road-level Flood Sensing for Disruption Assessment based on Uncertainties and Bayesian Networks
abstract: Urban flooding severely disrupts road traffic, and assessing these disruptions in a near real-time manner depends on road-level flood sensing that is usually constrained by limited financial and manpower resources. Therefore, positioning a limited number of sensing nodes requires valuing candidate locations. Yet existing strategies value locations mainly by traffic volume or local flood severity rather than disruption, and consider roads in isolation, overlooking how disruption propagates between connected roads. This study builds a double-layered Bayesian network that couples roads through their flood and traffic dependencies. A flood observed at one road then propagates to the inferred traffic disruptions across the connected network. Each candidate location is scored by the Value of Information (VoI) it contributes, combining the magnitude of the revealed traffic disruptions with how far they depart from historical expectation. A greedy algorithm then places sensing nodes where this network-wide value is the greatest. In a New York City expressway case study, the network estimates traffic speeds and the relative levels of disruption, and a few well-placed sensing nodes capture most of the attainable value. The VoI-based positioning achieves higher accumulated value than heuristics based on flood probability, traffic volume, or disruption alone. The framework is expected to help transportation and emergency agencies deploy limited flood-sensing resources where they most improve real-time traffic disruption assessment during urban floods.

title: Gas leak source localization in complex environments using a multilevel simulated annealing Bayesian–MCMC framework
abstract: Accurate gas leak source localization is essential for industrial safety monitoring and emergency response under uncertain dispersion conditions. This study develops a Bayesian inversion framework that combines Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling with multilevel simulated annealing (MLSA) initialization. Evaluation was conducted entirely using simulated data, including idealized scenarios and FLACS generated industrial concentration fields. Across 50 independent executions of the principal idealized scenario, MLSA-BMCMC achieved lower mean localization and release rate errors than B-MCMC and SA-BMCMC. Repeated noise experiments indicated adequate credible interval calibration at noise levels of 10%-30%. The FLACS cases further characterized the influence of geometric complexity on localization performance. Overall, the proposed framework provides a structured refinement of Bayesian gas leak source inversion by combining coarse to fine initialization with posterior uncertainty quantification under the tested dispersion conditions.

title: A Hyper Graphical Evaluation and Review Technique Modeling Framework for Life-Cycle Reliability of Reusable Rockets
An Open-source Toolbox for Critical Infrastructure Generation and Resilience Analysis with Decision-Relevant Applications
abstract: Critical infrastructure resilience is central to modern society, and open-source resilience toolboxes are increasingly important as domain-specific simulation engines for automated and agent-assisted scientific analysis in the AI era. Existing toolboxes have enabled diverse single- and interdependent-system studies, but many rely on detailed infrastructure data, face calibration and validation challenges under sparse observations, or separate key decision factors across fragmented workflows. We develop an open-source MATLAB toolbox for Critical Infrastructure Generation and Resilience Analysis (CIGRA) that can synthesize or augment electric power, water, gas, and road networks from population maps and optional road data, and infer missing component-specific demand and flow attributes. CIGRA further enables the identification of worst-case localized and non-localized disruption scenarios, providing a stress-testing pathway when observations are insufficient for comprehensive calibration and validation and supporting worst-case-oriented resilience planning. These capabilities are integrated with hazard cascade and component-damage scenario generation, functionality-loss calculation, restoration simulation, multiscale resilience evaluation, resilience enhancement exploration, and visualization modules to support systematic “what-if” comparisons across hazard, operating, restoration, and intervention assumptions, together with optimization-based planning. Applications of the CIGRA demonstrate an end-to-end seismic resilience analysis, how resilience measures influence resilience rankings and retrofit priorities, and how system evolution can alter system-level resilience and influence the effectiveness of retrofit strategies. CIGRA is calibration-ready and openly available at https://github.com/CICR-Lab/CIGRA.

title: Risk response decisions for critical infrastructures in complex interdependent scenarios: A data-intelligence-driven integrated model
abstract: Critical infrastructures (CIs) are often exposed to multiple risks whose consequences may be aggravated or mitigated by both CI interdependency and risk interdependency, making the modeling of risk response decisions (RRDs) more challenging under limited and heterogeneous information. This study aims to develop a data-intelligence-driven RRD model that links preparedness, detection/diagnosis, and treatment decisions through a shared ontology representation. First, an RRD ontology is constructed from multi-source text data and expert knowledge to organize reusable scenario, criterion, strategy, and rule knowledge. Subsequently, a dual-interdependency and criterion-adaptive mechanism is employed to quantify the realistic scenario by combining predefined information with on-site observations and interdependency-effect information, in which aggregation is configured according to the interdependency and cumulative characteristics of individual criteria. Following the scenario diagnosis, ontology-based case retrieval is conducted, and the extracted strategies enter a rule-guided post-retrieval adaptation process involving effect screening, coverage checking, and strategy coordination. Furthermore, a case study on the “7.21 Beijing Torrential Rain” is conducted. Sensitivity, ablation, and retrospective analyses examine the local stability of the decision results, the effects of interdependency modeling and rule-guided adaptation, and the correspondence between generated actions and documented historical responses. This study provides case-specific evidence for the feasibility, incremental decision value, and practical relevance of the proposed model for RRDs in complex interdependent CI scenarios.

title: Mining of Fault Propagation Mechanisms in Computer Numerical Control Machine Tools via Information Fusion and Association Rules
abstract: Enhancing the reliability of CNC (Computer Numerical Control) machine tools requires precise identification of fault propagation paths. However, existing methods often treat macroscopic topology and microscopic mechanisms in isolation and suffer from biases inherent in single-source data. To address these issues, this paper proposes a reliability-oriented mechanism mining framework integrating information fusion and Association Rule Mining (ARM). First, a game-theoretic weighted Decision Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL)–Interpretive Structural Modeling (ISM) method is proposed to fuse expert knowledge with failure statistics. This constructs a robust hierarchical topology that mitigates data sparsity. Second, using this topology as a physical constraint, a constraint-based Apriori algorithm is developed. With downtime-centric constraints, it extracts microscopic failure mechanisms from abstract paths. It also overcomes the limitations of traditional algorithms in capturing temporal logic and fault chains. A case study on a five-axis machining center identifies the Electrical System as the most influential subsystem within the identified fault propagation topology and the Automatic Tool Changer (ATC) as the most susceptible unit. The proposed method detects latent High-Impact Low-Probability (HILP) chains and improves Precision, Recall, and F1-score by 2.56 ×, 1.75 ×, and 2.16 × over the traditional algorithm. These results demonstrate improved consistency with the topology-constrained reference patterns for reliability diagnosis of complex electromechanical systems.

title: An Overlap-Aware Rectification Deep Neural Network with Dual-Branch Architecture for Gearbox Open-Set Fault Diagnosis
abstract: Open-set fault diagnosis (OSFD) requires accurate recognition of known faults while rejecting unseen fault categories, but feature overlap near decision boundaries can cause both false rejection and false acceptance. This study proposes an Overlap-Aware Rectification Network (OAR-Net) that combines multi-scale feature extraction, dual-branch metric learning, and a three-stage decision strategy. Samples with clear Mahalanobis-distance evidence are directly accepted or rejected, whereas samples in the intermediate buffer region are further evaluated using prediction uncertainty, local manifold inconsistency, inter-class distance ambiguity, and boundary position. Experiments on the Southeast University (SEU) and Chongqing University (CQU) gearbox datasets show that OAR-Net achieves average OA, UDR, and F1 values of 98.93%, 99.32%, and 99.13%, respectively, on SEU, and 99.01%, 99.31%, and 98.99%, respectively, on CQU. On SEU, OAR-Net improves average OA and F1 by 2.52 and 2.61 percentage points, respectively, over FDML, the strongest baseline by average OA. Cross-speed experiments further show that OAR-Net maintains relatively stable performance under smaller speed variations, although performance degrades as the speed discrepancy increases. These results support the effectiveness of overlap-aware staged verification for gearbox OSFD.

title: OceanPathRL: Deep reinforcement learning-based energy-efficient route optimization system for autonomous electric vessels
abstract: Autonomous electric vessels operating in complex maritime environments must simultaneously optimize energy consumption, maintain regulatory compliance, and coordinate with multiple vessels in real time, yet no existing framework addresses all three objectives within a unified learning architecture. This paper presents OceanPathRL, a novel deep reinforcement learning framework for energy-efficient route optimization in autonomous electric vessels. We propose a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning architecture that integrates Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) with attention-based neural networks and a COLREGs-compliant reward formulation to enable real-time path planning under dynamic ocean conditions, including wave energy prediction and photovoltaic uncertainty management. Extensive evaluations on two publicly available benchmarks, namely the Singapore Maritime Dataset and the MarineCadastre AIS dataset, demonstrate that OceanPathRL achieves a 34.7% reduction in energy consumption compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining a 99.2% collision avoidance success rate and 98.0% COLREGs compliance across head-on, crossing, overtaking, and multi-vessel encounter scenarios. The proposed meta-learning transfer mechanism reduces adaptation steps to new maritime environments by approximately 72.8% relative to conventional training, corresponding to a 3.68× average speedup. These results establish OceanPathRL as a practical and scalable solution for next-generation autonomous maritime systems, directly contributing to the International Maritime Organization decarbonization targets and advancing the field toward deployable, regulation-aware autonomous navigation.

title: DERF: Dynamic evolution risk field-based risk assessment for pedestrian-vehicle potential collision
abstract: Accurate and timely assessment of pedestrian-vehicle collision risk is fundamental to the reliability and safety assurance of autonomous driving systems. In urban traffic, inadequate modelling of pedestrian-vehicle interactions and lagging risk perception leave pedestrians vulnerable. To address this, the paper introduces a dynamic evolving risk field (DERF) method and develops a collision volume model using bounding boxes to enable effective trajectory crossing detection. Temporal risk is quantified by fusing time difference to collision and time to last arrival, while spatial risk is modelled via cusp catastrophe theory to capture nonlinear transitions from gradual to acute states. A multilayer perceptron nonlinearly fuses these features into spatiotemporal interaction factors, combined with a direction-sensitive modulation function, enabling real-time smooth evolution of risk field intensity and distribution. Experiments on the pedestrian-vehicle interaction dataset show that our method achieves 0.92 accuracy at a 1 s prediction horizon and 38.5 FPS, outperforming state-of-the-art in accuracy, recall, and operation speed. The results confirm that our approach delivers reliable risk estimates with balanced precision and recall, supporting reliable safety assessment under dynamic and uncertain traffic conditions.

title: Resilience-constrained power system capacity expansion planning considering cascading failures
abstract: Extreme weather events can trigger cascading failures and prolonged blackouts, threatening power system resilience. Resilience-oriented capacity expansion planning is complicated by the coupling among investment decisions, cascading failure evolution, and post-event restoration, as planning decisions reshape the pre-event dispatch and power flows, thereby affecting cascading trajectories and the initial blackout states for post-event restoration. To address this challenge, this study develops a resilience-constrained capacity expansion planning framework for generation and energy storage systems (ESSs) that jointly optimizes regional capacities and bus-level resource type, location, and quantity, while accounting for disaster-induced cascading failures and system restoration. A sequential AC power flow-based simulation model is employed to capture the dynamic evolution of system outages under severe disturbances. The framework incorporates black-start and load restoration constraints and considers coordinated operation of grid-forming and grid-following ESSs. Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) metrics are further introduced to control the tail risk of load shedding. An iterative optimization-simulation strategy is proposed to address the endogenous dependence between planning decisions and cascading failure evolution under extreme event uncertainty, followed by a verification stage to ensure risk constraints are satisfied under the scenarios induced by the planning scheme itself. Results on the modified IEEE 39-bus system show that the proposed plan reduces the total cost by 10.76% relative to the benchmark without planning-dependent cascading-failure updates, while maintaining surviving generation output above 80% across all 20 disaster scenarios. On the IEEE 118-bus system, the number of near-total blackout scenarios is reduced from six to two across the 20 scenarios.

title: A diffusion model-enhanced deep state-space model for RUL prediction
abstract: Multisensor degradation data typically exhibit high dimensionality, strong noise, and nonlinear evolution, which pose challenges to existing Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction methods in terms of degradation representation learning, temporal modeling, and predictive uncertainty quantification. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Diffusion-Enhanced Deep State-Space Model (Diff-SSM) trained under a two-stage strategy. In the first stage, a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) integrated with a convolutional block attention module (CBAM) is pretrained in a self-supervised manner to extract deep degradation representations that are robust to noise and sensitive to degradation evolution. In the second stage, the learned degradation representations drive a deep state-space model. Specifically, a gated recurrent unit (GRU) constructs the state equation to model temporal degradation evolution, while a variational autoencoder (VAE) constructs the observation equation by mapping the latent variable to the conditional distribution of RUL. Within a variational inference framework, the diffusion feature extractor and the deep state-space model are jointly optimized end-to-end, enabling unified learning of degradation representation extraction, temporal modeling, and RUL inference. Finally, Monte Carlo sampling yields RUL point estimates and prediction intervals. Experiments on the C-MAPSS and PHM2010 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Time-Dependent Reliability Analysis of Anchored Slopes Under Varying Seismic Intensities and Allowable Displacement Criteria
abstract: This study proposes an integrated time-variant reliability analysis framework incorporating varying seismic intensities and performance-based allowable displacement (AD) criteria. A 12-m-high anchored slope was investigated using four sets of non-stationary random ground motion samples with different Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) levels. The systematic analysis examined the influence of seismic intensity on slope acceleration response, anchor axial force variation, and permanent displacement characteristics. The Probability Density Evolution Method (PDEM) was used to track the probability density evolution of crest permanent displacement, quantifying time-varying failure probability under various displacement thresholds. The numerical framework is validated against a large-scale shaking-table test of an anchored slope and benchmarked against Monte Carlo simulation, jointly confirming the modeling accuracy and computational efficiency of the proposed approach. Results indicate that slope dynamic responses are highly sensitive to seismic intensity and exhibit significant spatial variability. Acceleration and permanent displacement are markedly amplified at the slope crest and surface compared to the interior. Strong motions increase response uncertainty, leading to nonlinear time-dependent displacement accumulation. Anchor axial forces exhibit significant spatial heterogeneity, with toe anchors sustaining the highest loads during high-intensity earthquakes. Failure probability is governed jointly by PGA and AD thresholds, while the mainshock phase constitutes a critical window for abrupt failure probability escalation. The study offers guidance for the seismic design and reliability assessment of anchored slopes in high-intensity regions.

title: A Two-Stage Bayesian Framework for Multi-Fidelity Sequential Updating of Spatial Fragility Fields
abstract: This paper develops a Bayesian framework for updating event-conditioned spatial fragility fields by combining physics-informed priors with incrementally available post-disaster observations. The framework supports sequential refinement of regional vulnerability estimates as additional post-disaster evidence becomes available. The framework reformulates physics-informed fragility estimates into a Probit–Normal (PN) representation that captures aleatory variability and epistemic uncertainty in an analytically tractable form. Stage 1 performs local Bayesian updating by moment-matching PN marginals to Beta surrogates that preserve their probability shapes, enabling conjugate Beta–Bernoulli updates with soft, multi-fidelity observations. Fidelity weights encode source reliability, and the resulting Beta posteriors are re-projected into PN form, producing heteroscedastic fragility estimates whose variances reflect data quality and coverage. Stage 2 assimilates the heteroscedastic pseudo-observations through an ordered probit-warped Gaussian Process (GP) that propagates information across space and structural archetypes. A shared latent spatial severity field and strictly positive threshold-gap functions enforce pathwise ordering of exceedance probabilities and yield nonnegative exact damage-state probabilities. The framework is applied to the 2011 Joplin tornado, where wind-field priors and computer-vision damage assessments are fused under varying assumptions about tornado width, sampling strategy, and observation completeness. Controlled synthetic experiments and the Joplin application show that the framework can reduce the influence of biased priors as evidence accumulates, propagate locally updated information into unobserved regions, and produce uncertainty-aware, ordinally valid exceedance and exact damage-state probability fields.

title: Evaluating the uncertainty anisotropy in flight trajectory prediction using Bayesian Neural Network and SHapley Additive exPlanations
abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is essential for flight trajectory prediction in safety-critical Air Traffic Control (ATC) systems. Existing uncertainty quantification methods for flight trajectory prediction often focus on overall uncertainty magnitude or prediction interval coverage, while the spatial anisotropy of predictive uncertainty remains insufficiently investigated. This study first provides empirical evidence that flight trajectory prediction uncertainty is inherently anisotropic, with substantially different uncertainty distributions across longitude, latitude, and altitude. Based on this observation, uncertainty anisotropy is introduced as a complementary evaluation dimension for assessing the quality of uncertainty quantification. A Bayesian Seq-Seq-LSTM framework is developed to jointly predict flight trajectories and quantify predictive uncertainty, and three anisotropy metrics are proposed to quantitatively evaluate the uncertainty anisotropy. Furthermore, SHAP is used to quantify the contributions of input features to model predictions, and the resulting feature-importance patterns are examined alongside the observed uncertainty anisotropy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves better prediction accuracy and uncertainty estimation. Compared with baseline models exhibiting either weak or extreme anisotropy, the proposed framework produces a more moderate degree of uncertainty anisotropy. These findings further demonstrate that uncertainty anisotropy can serve as a complementary evaluation criterion for assessing the physical consistency and reliability of uncertainty estimation in flight trajectory prediction models.

title: SMARF: a semantic memory compression and data-driven prototype-consistency reasoning framework for fault diagnosis based on edge-side small models
abstract: Reliable industrial fault diagnosis with small language models requires traceable evidence, effective retention of temporal context, and stable diagnostic decisions. This study proposes SMARF, a framework that coordinates semantic memory compression and prototype-consistency ranking under a limited context budget. Schema-constrained Semantic Logs link multimodal observations, operating states, and standardized residuals to their evidence sources. A diagnosis-specific memory hierarchy retains temporal evidence through condition-, trend-, and candidate-aware organization. Candidate diagnoses are ranked by combining semantic confidence, retrieved-memory relevance, and training-derived prototype consistency, while uncertainty-guided feedback directs subsequent evidence processing. Using Qwen3-1.7B, SMARF was evaluated on aviation-pump recordings and the UCI Hydraulic Systems dataset. Under 11-fold leave-one-file-out evaluation, SMARF correctly classified all 11 held-out files containing internal operating-state variation, matching the best comparison methods in file-level accuracy and achieving the lowest observed file-level log loss of 0.0538. Correct file decisions were maintained across ten tested seeds and five local sensitivity configurations. Under the strict grouped UCI protocol, SMARF achieved a task-average Macro-F1 of 0.861 across four component-state recognition tasks, with a 95% group-bootstrap confidence interval of [0.839, 0.881]. These results support the value of coordinated semantic memory and statistical consistency checks for fault diagnosis, combining accurate predictions with traceable intermediate evidence and stable decisions under the evaluated conditions.

title: Entropy Modelling of Hierarchical Structures and Systemic Risk
abstract: Hierarchical systems are usually complex, adaptive and have stochastic behavior. One of the pressing issues in the field of reliability of such systems is the problem of systemic risks, which refer to the risk of failure of the entire system, rather than simply the failure of its individual parts. Currently, systemic risk research is understudied, and adequate tools for its analysis and detection have yet to be developed. In this article, regarding hierarchical systems, we propose using the differential entropy of continuous random vectors, which is a fundamental characteristic of any system with stochastic behavior, as a tool for studying systemic risk. The entropy of a random vector is decomposed into two components, one of which characterizes chaos, and the other characterizes the interdependence between its elements. An interpretation of systemic risk in terms of entropy measures of randomness and dependence is given. All the main variants of correlation relationships in hierarchical systems are considered, including cross correlation between all elements, between subsystems at different levels of the system, and between one element and a group of elements. The simplicity of the analytical formulas allows for the practical application of the vector entropy model. Moreover, the proposed approach provides the opportunity of monitoring not only the entire system, but also its individual subsystems, which expands the possibilities of its practical use. Examples of Gaussian hierarchical systems are given, which demonstrate the possibility of using the entropy model for monitoring systemic risk.

title: A Novel Data-Model Dual-Driven Implicit Remaining Useful Life Prediction Method for Reusable Thin-Walled Structures
abstract: Accurate remaining useful life prediction for reusable thin-walled structures is challenging because of implicit health indicators and insufficient monitoring data. To address this issue, this study proposes a data-model dual-driven implicit RUL prediction method. First, a distance correlation-based feature mapping method is developed to transform high-dimensional monitoring responses into low-dimensional features that are strongly correlated with implicit load-carrying capacity degradation. Second, a triple-uncertainty adaptive Wiener process is introduced to identify nonlinear degradation trajectories without prespecifying their functional forms, while quantifying random effects, temporal uncertainty, and measurement uncertainty. Subsequently, degradation function-constrained calibration of intrinsic structural parameters is performed, enabling indirect monitoring data to inversely update the high-fidelity structural model. Furthermore, a multi-fidelity Gaussian process model and a discrepancy correction model are employed to predict future structural performance and quantify RUL uncertainty. The results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively captures nonlinear implicit degradation, improves long-term prediction accuracy under limited monitoring data, and provides uncertainty-aware RUL estimates. This method provides an interpretable and physically constrained approach for life prediction and maintenance decision-making of reusable thin-walled structures.

title: Spatio-temporal task selection and mission abort decisions during multi-task execution under stochastic degradation
abstract: This study investigates a degrading mobile system that sequentially executes multiple spatially distributed tasks, while balancing the conflicting objectives of mission success and system survival. Mission abort policies define conditions under which a mission should be aborted to avoid severe economic losses and safety hazards caused by system failure. In many real-world missions, particularly those involving a single system performing sequential tasks, the ability to adapt both task sequences and abort timing in response to real-time system health is critical. However, relatively few studies have investigated mission abort policies in such multi-task settings. In this study, each task is represented as a position vector on a two-dimensional plane, and the mission trajectory is discretized into equal-length segments using a predefined spatial interval, thereby generating regular decision epochs along the execution path. Decision-making is based on the system state, including the degradation level, current position, and task progress. The focus of this study is on integrating intermediate mission abort decisions with dynamic task selection in a multi-task setting. This framework enables dynamic decisions between task continuation and mission abort during execution, as well as between task selection and mission abort at task completion. The resulting problem is formulated as a Markov decision process, and the value functions are explicitly derived to characterize the optimal policy. The structural properties of the optimal policy are established, including the monotonicity of the value function and the degradation-threshold structure of the mission abort decision under a safe-return assumption. Extensive sensitivity analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed policy across different parameter settings, spatial layouts, and numbers of tasks, while providing evidence of its robustness and computational scalability over the problem settings considered.

title: Human-centred risk assessment for port operations using a data-driven approach
abstract: Port operations are undergoing rapid digitalisation and automation, yet existing port safety studies remain limited in explaining how human, organisational, and machinery-related factors contribute to different casualty types. This study identifies key contributing risk factors in reported port accidents and develops an exploratory quantitative framework for casualty-type analysis. Using 77 historical accident reports as the development dataset, an accident-report-driven framework integrating LASSO regression with a Tree-Augmented Naive Bayes (TAN) network was constructed. Separate bootstrap stability assessments, repeated nested cross-validation, and supplementary external assessment were conducted. The study makes three contributions: (1) it identifies risk-factor patterns associated with different casualty types; (2) it applies a LASSO–TAN framework to model conditional dependencies among selected factors; (3) it conducts scenario analysis to support casualty-specific accident interpretation and hypothesis generation. The results indicate that equipment type, safeguards, cargo type, safety warnings, and ergonomic conditions are the principal predictors retained within the analysed dataset. Machinery-related injury and fall-from-height MPE configurations share container cargo, unclear warnings, poor ergonomic conditions, and non-adopted safeguards, but differ in equipment type. The findings support retrospective accident interpretation rather than accident-occurrence prediction or claims of intervention effectiveness.

title: Design of robust multiple-layer networks for unmanned aerial vehicle communication systems
abstract: A multiple-layer UAV system includes multiple types of UAVs, and different types of UAVs are at different layers. Network robustness is used to measure the connectivity of remaining network after some nodes fail. A highly robust network can ensure that UAVs can still communicate with each other even after some UAVs fail. To improve robustness of multi-layer UAVs network, we propose a method that combines positions of UAVs and network topology. The method can be divided into two sub-methods: flight strategy and network structure. In the flight strategy, an intra-layer potential field and an inter-layer potential field are used to adjust positions of UAVs under constraints, which can reduce distance between UAVs and can enable UAVs to establish more links. Although increasing links can improve the robustness of network, the dependence of network on critical nodes has greatly increased. Once these nodes fail, the robustness of network sharply decreases. In the network structure, Deep learning method is used to search for highly robust network structure. The designed deep learning method can evenly distribute links across nodes while increasing links, thereby reducing the impact of critical nodes on network. In 3D space, experimental results show that our method can meet constraints of multi-layer UAVs network, and enables networks to have high robustness in multiple failure modes.

title: A Multi-Level Dependability Model for Structural Degradation Composition and Resource Prioritisation in Cybersecurity Service Networks
abstract: Dependability assessment of interconnected service infrastructures requires the local degradation of individual services to be integrated with the structural dependencies through which their system-wide effects accumulate. Existing approaches typically analyse queueing performance, resilience, structural criticality, and resource allocation separately, thereby providing limited support for compositional system-level assessment. This study proposes a multi-level dependability model for an open network of cybersecurity services that combines local stochastic dynamics, routing-weighted structural degradation composition, and cost-aware resource reinforcement. Each service is represented as a hysteresis-controlled GI/M/1 node with renewal arrivals and two-rate exponential service. Local stationary degradation measures are transformed through a non-negative compositional network operator to obtain a global degradation functional and a normalised dependability indicator. A structural-functional sensitivity criterion is then derived to prioritise service reinforcement according to the predicted reduction in global degradation per unit cost. Controlled local verification using renewal inputs matched to node-level arrival summaries from CIC-IDS2017 and UNSW-NB15 yielded a Spearman correlation of 0.99983 and a mean absolute error of 0.00579 events for the time-stationary mean number in the system. Relative to a resource-equivalent fixed-rate model, median relative error decreased from 11.8% to 5.0% and from 13.9% to 5.8%. The proposed framework provides an analytically grounded basis for dependability assessment and resource prioritisation in structurally interdependent service networks.

title: How Do Hazard–Exit–Behavior Interactions Amplify Risk in Classroom Earthquake Evacuation?
abstract: Classroom earthquake evacuation is a time-critical safety problem because evolving non-structural hazards can simultaneously constrain exit functionality and alter pedestrian responses. Existing models often treat environmental hazards, exit conditions, and adaptive behavior separately, limiting their ability to explain how localized seismic disruption propagates into congestion and hazard exposure. This study develops a mechanism-oriented hazard–exit–behavior coupling framework integrating fragility-driven hazard generation, time-varying exit-capacity degradation, stress-responsive movement adjustment, utility-based exit choice, and dynamic path replanning. The framework is evaluated through empirical speed–density comparison, adaptive-speed ablation, component-level verification, and progressive coupling comparison. Results show that seismic excitation alone causes limited degradation, whereas falling hazards substantially increase evacuation delay and exposure. The 95th-percentile evacuation time rises from 15.46 s in the baseline and dynamic-hazard-only cases to 56.73 s with exit degradation and 81.70 s under full coupling. Meanwhile, 95th-percentile hazard exposure decreases from 51.14 s to 47.89 s from exit degradation to full coupling, indicating behavioral redistribution of congestion and exposure. Hazards concentrated near exits cause greater degradation than spatially dispersed hazards. These findings identify a risk-amplification pathway linking localized hazards, exit degradation, behavioral adaptation, and congestion evolution.

title: Incentivized Coordinated Resilient Scheduling for Multi-Microgrids: An Asymmetric Nash Bargaining Approach Considering Peer-to-Peer Trading and Differentiated Demand Response
abstract: Extreme events may force interconnected multi-microgrid systems into islanded operation, resulting in severe power shortages and operational challenges. Under such conditions, enabling resilient and incentive-compatible cooperation among self-interested microgrids through peer-to-peer trading remains an important research issue. To this end, a coordinated resilient scheduling framework based on asymmetric Nash bargaining is proposed for interconnected multi-microgrids, incorporating differentiated demand response to exploit the heterogeneous flexibility of data center batch workloads, industrial processes, and thermostatically controlled loads. The proposed framework consists of a social welfare maximization problem and a profit allocation problem, where asymmetric bargaining factors are introduced to reflect the contributions of participating microgrids. A tailored projection function based alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is further developed to solve the resulting mixed-integer nonlinear programming problem in a distributed manner while preserving microgrid privacy. Case studies on the IEEE 33-bus and IEEE 123-bus systems show that the proposed framework effectively reduces operating costs and load shedding, verifying its effectiveness and scalability.

title: Optimal condition-based maintenance and inspection strategy under imperfect condition monitoring: Relevance of the partially observable Markov decision process framework
abstract: Condition-based maintenance (CBM) strategies rely on the condition monitoring of a given asset to schedule maintenance interventions. In this article, we focus on a system with multiple degraded states and seek to compute the optimal CBM policy when two sources of monitoring information are available to the decision-maker. On the one hand, we consider that a continuous monitoring system is implemented, providing free but imperfect information. On the other hand, the decision-maker may decide to schedule costly but perfect inspections, revealing exactly the true degradation state of the item. We model the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where preventive maintenance actions should be wisely planned in order to reduce the likelihood of expensive failures and corrective maintenance interventions. We show that the POMDP framework is a convenient way when dealing with imperfect information. POMDP may be difficult to solve, but we compare two concurrent solving approaches and illustrate to what extent modern solvers have improved and enabled them to solve such problems efficiently. Finally, we propose a sensitivity analysis on the performance of the condition monitoring system and suggest that such a framework could be very helpful in estimating the value of information (VoI) that could be expected from the implementation of sensing technologies with a certain average accuracy. We further quantify the value of perfect inspections and show that monitoring and inspections act as substitutes.

title: A two-stage deep causal inference method with association prior for urban rail transit risk impact deduction and proactive intervention
abstract: To enhance the in-time safety management capability of urban rail transit, this paper proposes a two-stage deep causal inference framework with association prior for causal discovery and interpretable intervention in risk impact deduction. Firstly, the association rules obtained by the improved W-apriori algorithm are transformed into prior matrix, allowing causal weight to be estimated in the feasible risk evolution space and bridging the gap between statistical mining and causal inference. Next, a five-layer causal topology is reconstructed using AP-DAG-GNN, with high-weight causal relationship extracted by Pareto optimization. Then, Causal-DEMATEL and DWBC are designed to analyze node-level topological features and path-level causal cascades. Moreover, event-specific causal attribution is developed for interpretable analysis of individual high-risk emergency, identifying key causal evolution pathways and intervention nodes. To demonstrate the proposed framework, six event types are simulated using real operational data from Beijing Metro combined with baseline comparison, ablation experiment and structural stability analysis, which indicates that high-weight causal topology selected by Pareto is sensitive to random optimization and finite sample perturbations, while some key causal relationships exhibit relatively high recurrence and node importance ranking exhibits a certain degree of event dependency. These findings can not only support the effectively identification of stable risk propagation pathways and candidate intervention priorities, but also sensitively capture causal center shifts caused by specific conditions, thereby providing a foundation for early intervention, warning release, and implementation of proactive risk prevention and control strategies.

title: Weather-aware anomaly detection for ship behavior based on Transformer
abstract: Anomaly detection in ship behavior is crucial for maritime safety and intelligent shipping systems. However, the weather conditions surrounding the ship are typically neglected by existing anomaly detection methods. In this study, a Weather-Aware Ship Anomaly Detection (WASAD) model is proposed to enhance ship anomaly detection by incorporating real weather conditions from ERA5 reanalysis data aligned with AIS trajectories. First, AIS trajectories are spatiotemporally aligned with ERA5 weather data using cubic spline interpolation, followed by bilinear interpolation. The data are subsequently mapped into high-dimensional embeddings. A gated fusion module is then utilized to adaptively adjust the weights of environmental influences. Complex long-term spatiotemporal dependencies within the behavior patterns are captured by a six-layer Transformer encoder. Finally, anomalies are precisely identified by evaluating context-modulated anomaly scores. The model is validated using real-world AIS data combined with ERA5 data. Under all weather conditions, an anomaly detection accuracy exceeding 98% is achieved by the proposed framework, and the False Positive Rate is reduced to approximately 1.2%. This framework could be used to enhance intelligent maritime surveillance, thereby improving the safety and reliability of autonomous navigation systems.

title: Reliable virtual sensing of inter-turbine total pressure in degraded aero-engines via physics-constrained online learning
abstract: Reliable acquisition of inter-turbine total pressure P43 remains difficult in aero-engines, especially under component degradation and anomalous data conditions. This study proposes a physics-constrained virtual sensing method for reliable reconstruction of P43 in degraded aero-engines. First, building on rotor-inertia-power-balance-based temperature reconstruction, the underlying assumptions and degradation-induced mismatch characteristics of forward and backward P43 reconstruction are analyzed, and P43 is rapidly reconstructed using measurable low-temperature-region parameters and engine design information. Second, the physical reconstruction is embedded into an online sequential extreme learning machine to establish a physics-constrained learning framework. An adaptive data-physics fusion strategy and an online regression mechanism are further introduced to improve robustness under degradation, anomalous training data, and previously unseen operating conditions. Comparative simulations show that the proposed method maintains relatively low reconstruction errors under the considered degradation conditions and exhibits reduced sensitivity to physical-model mismatch compared with the evaluated physics-based and hybrid baselines. It also suppresses the influence of noisy and biased data, reduces the dependence on a high-dimensional fault-sample database, and provides stable prediction over a wide operating envelope with low computational cost. These results indicate that the proposed method offers a practical and reliable solution for monitoring degradation-sensitive parameters in complex aero-engine systems.

title: A risk-aware surrogate Bayesian optimization framework driven by spatial generalized extreme value model for urban road network simulation calibration
abstract: Traffic simulation serves as a prerequisite support for the engineering application of research in the safety domain in urban road networks. To reproduce the spatial crash risk field, calibrating traffic simulations at the urban road network level is a complex and systematic task. Challenges remain in replicating traffic safety via such simulations, especially when safety is dominated by extreme vehicle interactions rather than average traffic conflicts. Generally, the spatial heterogeneity of crash risk in urban road networks is mainly associated with origin-destination demand, extreme traffic conflicts, and driver behavior. However, existing methods often consider these factors independently, which limits their ability to capture spatial crash risk patterns. Given this, this study proposes a risk-aware surrogate Bayesian optimization framework driven by spatial generalized extreme value model for urban road network simulation calibration. This framework considers origin-destination demand representation, spatial extreme crash risk modeling, and heterogeneous driver behavior calibration. The results show that: (i) the framework ensures consistency between simulated and observed traffic volumes; (ii) it improves the fidelity of extreme events by reproducing the lower tail of traffic conflict distributions. From a systematic perspective, this study serves as a pioneering study for the coordinated control oriented toward safety and resilience.

title: Optimal maintenance and abort policies for mission-critical systems with heterogeneous mission severity
abstract: Many mission-critical systems must complete an ordered sequence of missions under uncertain deterioration and mission-dependent operating severity. Before each mission, the operator may start directly, perform maintenance to restore system health, or abort the remaining sequence. For heterogeneous mission profiles, the decision is difficult because mission severity affects failure risk, the post-mission health distribution, and the value of repairing the system for later missions. Existing studies optimize mission abort or maintenance separately, with limited attention to their joint design in multi-mission sequences with varying severity. This study develops a joint maintenance and mission abort policy for a mission-critical system subject to multiple heterogeneous missions. We formulate the problem as a finite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP) and derive structural properties showing that the optimal value is monotone in system health and mission severity, the abort decision follows a threshold structure, and severity changes the relative attractiveness of maintenance and direct continuation. Based on these properties, we develop an improved backward induction algorithm that prunes unnecessary state–action evaluations. Numerical examples show that the proposed policy achieves a lower expected total cost than benchmark policies, while the improved algorithm reduces computation time across the tested problem sizes.

title: Physics-informed shield attitude prediction and uncertainty-aware safety regulation: conformal-calibrated robust control barrier functions
abstract: Accurate shield-attitude prediction and reliable safety regulation are essential for intelligent tunneling, yet existing methods often lack physical consistency, calibrated uncertainty, and effective uncertainty propagation into safety control. This study proposes an integrated framework combining a Physics-Informed State Space Model (PI-SSM), trajectory-level conformal prediction, and a Conformal-Calibrated Robust Control Barrier Function (CC-RCBF). The PI-SSM adopts physically meaningful state-space initialization and non-invasive Generalized Spring-Mass-Damper (G-SMD) calibration, while a physics-anchored multi-horizon structure mitigates recursive error accumulation. Predictive uncertainty is quantified using a validation-weighted deep ensemble and calibrated by trajectory-level conformal prediction with causal sequential adaptation. The calibrated uncertainty is further incorporated into an energy-based CC-RCBF for actuator-constrained safety filtering. Using 50,857 operational samples from the Qingdao Second Sub-sea Tunnel, the proposed model achieves one-step R2 values of 0.9783 and 0.9789, and retains 0.9504 and 0.9173 at a 20-step horizon. The predictive performance of the PI-SSM is further validated using operational data from another shield tunneling alignment within the same project. G-SMD calibration reduces the physical residual by approximately three orders of magnitude, while CC-RCBF eliminates observed physical-limit violations in reduced-order stress testing and increases the minimum clearance to 0.92 mm. The framework is further integrated into a shield-attitude safety decision-support platform.

title: A vessel trajectory abnormal behavior classification method for cross-domain generalization and local motion pattern similarity mitigation
abstract: This paper investigates the classification of three typical anomalous maneuvering behaviors from AIS trajectories, namely looping, double U-turn, and low-speed dwelling. Such behaviors are closely associated with potential navigational risks and illicit maritime activities, and their accurate identification is essential for maritime surveillance. However, anomalous maneuvering behaviors often share similar local motion patterns while differing in global structure, leading to confusion among behavioral categories. Moreover, existing deep learning methods rely heavily on domain-specific data distributions, limiting reliability across heterogeneous maritime environments. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a vessel trajectory classification framework that improves cross-domain generalization and reduces behavioral ambiguity. The model adopts a dual-branch architecture to jointly capture local temporal dynamics and global geometric structure. A branch-level attention mechanism is further introduced to adaptively fuse the two branches, thereby alleviating the behavioral confusion caused by similar local motion patterns. To address cross-domain distribution shifts, a meta-learning training paradigm and an adaptation strategy optimized for few-shot multi-step updating are introduced, improving cross-domain adaptation in a closed-set setting where the source and target domains share a common class label space. Experiments are conducted on three cross-domain transfer scenarios. The results show that, under strong domain shift, the proposed method achieves the best performance among the compared methods while using only a few labels per class. Compared with domain adaptation and domain generalization methods that do not use target-domain labels, the proposed method attains comparable accuracy under weak shift, whereas under strong shift it achieves superior results with only a few labels.

title: Simulating dynamic transport-economic interdependencies for post-earthquake regional economic recovery
abstract: Infrastructure disruptions from natural hazards can generate substantial indirect economic losses through complex, time-dependent interdependencies between physical systems and regional economies. Systematic quantification of these propagation mechanisms is essential for developing actionable mitigation and recovery strategies that maximize societal benefits. This study develops a dynamic modeling framework that explicitly links transport system disruptions, including road networks and ports, to regional economic performance through physical constraints on labor and freight mobility. The framework integrates hazard simulation, physical system damage and recovery modeling, and a refined Adaptive Regional Input–Output (R-ARIO) model to dynamically simulate sectoral economic activities as physical disruptions evolve over time. We apply the framework to evaluate the indirect economic impacts of transport system disruption in the San Francisco Bay Area under a magnitude 7.3 Hayward earthquake scenario. Besides the direct building damage of $47.9 billion, the model estimates that transport system disruption can generate an additional $3.3 billion indirect economic loss on top of the $62.3 billion indirect loss attributed to building damage. Road network and port disruptions exhibit distinct temporal effects on regional economic performance, with varying sensitivities across economic sectors. Moreover, the physics-based integration enables the identification of sector-specific bottlenecks and associated critical periods introduced by each transport system during recovery, providing actionable insights for targeted mitigation and resilience planning to reduce cascading economic impacts.

Causal Contrastive Learning for Reliability-oriented Fault Detection in Wastewater Treatment under Process Uncertainty
abstract: To ensure reliable operations and quality control in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), data-driven fault detection has received wide attention recently, but reliable detection of faults or failures with respect to process variables or quality-related variables remains challenging due to significant process uncertainty. In WWTPs, fault detection is usually affected by data uncertainty, operating-condition uncertainty, and inter-variable relationship uncertainty. These uncertainties are essentially caused by delayed water-quality measurements, wastewater influent loads, or other environmental factors, such as temperature and humidity. In response to these issues, this study proposes causal structure contrastive learning (CSCL) for reliable WWTPs fault detection. In this method, CSCL addresses observation uncertainty by learning window-level representations rather than relying on isolated delayed measurements. Also, it can handle operating-condition uncertainty through causality-preserving augmentation, which retains normal causal structures under admissible influent and process variations. Furthermore, inter-variable relationship uncertainty, by constructing causality-disrupted negative samples that break internal causal dependencies or perturb exogenous-disturbance-driven causal patterns, can be addressed efficiently. By comparing causality-consistent with causality-disrupted samples, CSCL can separate normal process variability from fault-induced causal changes, thereby strengthening the reliability of fault detection. Experiments on BSM2 fault scenarios and full-scale WWTP data demonstrate that CSCL can outperform other fault detection baselines.

Neural Scheduling for Carrier Aircraft Recovery with Bolter and Aerial Refueling
abstract: Existing carrier aircraft recovery scheduling studies commonly assume a predetermined aircraft set, limiting their applicability to safety-critical operations involving bolter events, fuel-endurance risk, and online insertion of new-wave tasks. This study formulates dynamic carrier aircraft recovery scheduling as an event-driven sequential decision-making problem that jointly considers bolter recovery, aerial refueling, remaining-fuel evolution, and online task insertion. A Long-Range Dependency-Aware Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm, termed LDA-PPO, is developed by integrating a dynamic recovery pool with a multi-layer masking mechanism. The pool maps time-varying aircraft sets to a stable neural decision interface. The dynamic-recovery-pool and attention masks exclude empty slots from representation learning, while the action-feasibility mask excludes unavailable aircraft from action selection. Each aircraft is encoded as an aircraft token, and multi-head self-attention captures global dependencies in fuel safety, mechanical integrity, mission priority, bolter risk, and new-wave arrivals. In 128 single-wave scenarios with 32 aircraft, LDA-PPO combined higher mean composite objectives and low online computational cost with fewer touchdown fuel-reserve violations and better fuel reliability than most baselines. It handled different task sizes within the dynamic recovery pool capacity and multi-wave missions without parameter updates. The proposed method provides a reliability-oriented online decision-support framework for dynamic carrier aircraft recovery.

title: Pseudo-Anomaly Data Driven Robust and Confidence Information Redundancy Approach in Aircraft Components
abstract: Information redundancy (IR) for flight parameters requires robustness to corrupted auxiliary measurements and confidence assessment of the resulting estimates. This paper proposes a Pseudo-Anomaly data-driven Robust and Confidence IR (PA-RCIR) framework. A Random Anomaly Scenario Generator (RASG) generates pseudo-anomalous auxiliary inputs through complementary signal-level perturbations while preserving their target references. A Dual-phase Robust Variational Inference Network (DRVIN) jointly learns from original and perturbed inputs using a probabilistic latent representation. An Empirical Cumulative Distribution function of prediction Statistical Features (ECDSF) constructs empirical confidence scores from repeated prediction samples and a normal-validation reference distribution. Experiments use real flight records from the Thor and Ibis UAV datasets, with angle-of-attack (AoA) redundancy as a representative task and separate training and evaluation on each dataset. Over ten runs, the mean absolute error (MAE) under normal inputs is 0.0120 on Thor and 0.0007 on Ibis. Under controlled bias and noise corruptions affecting five auxiliary-input channels, the corresponding values are 0.0200 and 0.0012. In both evaluated multichannel mixed-anomaly scenarios, PA-RCIR achieves statistically significant improvements over all six baselines for the three prediction-error metrics after Holm correction. Representative cases and expected calibration error analysis characterize the relationship between confidence scores and prediction quality, with calibration behavior varying across input conditions and prediction-sample statistics. These results support robust information redundancy with empirical confidence assessment under the evaluated input conditions.

Human–AI Teaming Reliability in Diagnostic Tasks: Performance-Shaping Factors and Quantitative Modeling
abstract: Humans and AI systems are increasingly forming human–AI teaming configurations for operating complex safety-critical systems. Understanding and quantifying human–AI teaming reliability is therefore essential for system safety, yet it remains overlooked despite extensive research on human–AI teaming. Here we investigate certain key performance-shaping factors (PSFs) influencing teaming reliability and develop data-driven quantitative models. We focus on an important workflow in which humans make final decisions while AI provides advice in simulated medical diagnosis. In a preregistered behavioral experiment (N = 420), we measure human reliability and human–AI teaming reliability at two time points separated by one week. We manipulate AI reliability, task difficulty, and teaming mode (simultaneous vs. sequential), while exploring the roles of human baseline ability (lower vs. higher performers) and decision-making style (conservative vs. aggressive decision-makers). Results show that AI reliability and teaming mode affect human reliability gains from AI assistance. Sequential mode (humans access AI advice after forming initial judgments) yields greater reliability gains than simultaneous mode (humans access diagnostic cases and AI advice concurrently), with exploratory analyses suggesting that this advantage may be limited to aggressive decision-makers. We finally build two linear and nonlinear models of teaming reliability. Our findings advance the understanding of PSFs and quantitative modeling for human–AI teaming reliability.

Context-Aware Prompt Encoding Compression and Sentence-Level Pooling based LLMs for Industrial Equipment Health Status Prediction
abstract: Accurate forecasting of industrial equipment health states is crucial for improving system reliability, enabling predictive maintenance, and supporting intelligent manufacturing. Conventional forecasting methods primarily rely on structured sensor data and often fail to leverage reliability-related knowledge contained in unstructured sources such as maintenance reports and failure logs. Although large language models (LLMs) show strong capabilities in textual understanding, their application to industrial prognostics and health management remains limited due to weak integration with quantitative signals and sensitivity to irrelevant textual information. To address these issues, this study proposes a cross-modal forecasting framework, Context-Aware Prompt Encoding Compression and Sentence-Level Pooling–Large Language Model (CASP-LLM). The framework integrates maintenance text with sensor time-series data to improve equipment health-state prediction. Prompts derived from statistical characteristics of sensor signals guide context-aware encoding and sentence-level pooling to extract reliability-relevant semantic features, while a parallel pathway captures temporal degradation patterns from sensor observations. The resulting representations are fused for prediction. Experiments are conducted on public fuel cell datasets and two real industrial heat exchanger datasets. The results demonstrate that CASP-LLM consistently outperforms LSTM, Transformer, TimeLLM, and other comparative models across multiple forecasting horizons.

Uncertainty-aware dynamic-static knowledge injection for few-shot electromagnetic interference failure assessment via large language models
abstract: Electromagnetic interference (EMI) can reduce the reliability of electronic systems and lead to functional failures, making EMI immunity assessment essential for reliable system operation. However, such assessment usually requires many experiments, and the resulting data are often costly or unavailable. This makes few-shot EMI failure assessment difficult, especially when model uncertainty must be controlled and physical constraints must be respected. To address the above issues, we propose the Dynamic-Static Knowledge Injection Large Language Model (DSKI-LLM) for few-shot EMI failure assessment. The framework contains a static knowledge injection module and an uncertainty-aware dynamic module. The static module combines Domain-Corrective Alignment Loss with gated low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to encourage representations consistent with electromagnetic knowledge. The dynamic module uses predictive entropy to estimate confidence and adjusts retrieval depth during inference. Low-confidence queries retrieve more historical EMI cases, while high-confidence queries avoid unnecessary context expansion. We evaluate DSKI-LLM on PhyEMI, a benchmark dataset built from a controlled EMI experimental platform. Results show that DSKI-LLM improves few-shot prediction over the evaluated baselines and produces more reliable probability estimates. By combining prediction with uncertainty estimation and adaptive evidence retrieval, the proposed method supports more trustworthy EMI failure assessment under limited data.

title: Quality-aware LLM root-cause analysis of offshore incident reports: report quality as an upstream uncertainty in safety analytics
abstract: Incident reports are increasingly analyzed with large language models (LLMs), yet most studies treat report text as a fixed input. This study examines report quality as an upstream uncertainty in automated root cause analysis (RCA): whether the available record conditions what causal evidence can be recovered, how LLM-RCA models behave, and what safety narrative becomes visible. Using 1,000 public offshore incident records from BSEE, we develop an auditable LLM-assisted ranking pipeline that harmonizes heterogeneous reports, constructs an interpretable weak prior, aggregates listwise judgments with a regularized Bradley–Terry (BT) model, and incorporates targeted human pairwise calibration. The resulting quality prior is stable, with 99.985% of reports remaining within ±1 stratum under bootstrap perturbation. We then evaluate 250 Q-stratified incidents using a human-reviewed reference set and five GPT-5-mini runs. Mean top-level reference labels increase from 1.10 in Q1 to 3.38 in Q5, indicating richer recoverable RCA evidence. GPT-5-mini precision and F1 generally improve with quality; the model also under-abstains on sparse low-quality records. Report quality further conditions the recoverable safety narrative: low-quality reports emphasize personnel performance and external triggers, whereas high-quality reports reveal organizational and systemic contributors. These findings suggest that report quality is a first-order variable in LLM-based safety analytics.

title: AI-Enabled construction safety management: A paradigm shift from passive compliance to proactive empowerment
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to construction safety through hazard recognition, risk assessment, monitoring, and decision support. Despite rapid advances, existing systems differ substantially in their ability to interpret risk, generate safety-related outputs, and assume intervention authority. This study develops a reliability-oriented maturity framework to classify AI-enabled construction-safety functions. A PRISMA-guided review identified 171 eligible publications, including 153 technical studies and 18 reviews. The technical studies were characterized using two complementary dimensions: Objective Scanning Response (OSR), describing risk-information processing, and Safety State Output (SSO), describing safety-related output. Building on these functional profiles, an L0-L5 maturity framework is developed to characterize functional position, intervention authority, Operational Design Domain, and fallback capability. A Perception-Cognition-Decision-Execution (P-C-D-E) architecture is further developed to represent the functional structure of closed-loop safety intervention, including fast-slow functional separation, state verification, and fallback. Representative scenarios illustrate the framework’s application. The coded evidence indicates a marked asymmetry between risk understanding and physical intervention. The framework remains theoretically derived and has not undergone independent maturity-classification validation. Its contribution is nonetheless substantive: it provides a reproducible classification procedure, an authority-allocation model, and a reliability-oriented evaluation pathway specifying the evidence required before higher levels of autonomous intervention can be justified.

Reliability Analysis and Diagnosis of Million-Scale k-out-of-n Systems: O(k²) Constant-Space Forward Inference and Sliding-Window Reverse Diagnosis via the Noisy-Looper Bayesian Framework
